initial_presentation: A 58-year-old white male presented with numerous warty growths on his hands and feet. These lesions began appearing at the age of eight and have progressively increased in size over time. The patient has a history of an unspecified arrhythmia but is not on any medication. Family history indicates that the patient's father had similar skin lesions. Dermatological examination revealed multiple brownish, flat-topped warty plaques on the hands and feet, along with nail dystrophy.

The subject is a 15-year-old female who was delivered at full-term by parents who are not related by blood. Her birth weight was 2.2 kg, placing her in the 3rd percentile. She exhibited excessive hair growth starting at the age of 5 years. From the age of 13 years, she experienced the development of secondary sexual characteristics and rapid growth, but she has not yet had her first menstrual period. Her body mass index (BMI) is 18.4 kg/m2.

The patient, an 11-year-old female, has experienced short stature for 6 years prior to hospital admission. She is the fifth child of a nonconsanguineous couple. She was born naturally at full term with low birth weight and height and was breastfed. From the age of 5, her height has been below that of her peers.

The study received approval from the Cyprus National Bioethics Committee, and informed, written consent was obtained from all participants. The subject is a 30-year-old male weight lifter who presented with sudden onset chest and back pain. Initial assessment revealed no observable phenotypic features such as iris flocculi, livedo reticularis, or aortic valve abnormalities.

A 61-year-old female was referred for evaluation. Her medical history includes diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Initial symptoms began at age 21 with shoulder girdle weakness and subsequent difficulty walking. Physical examination revealed winged scapulae, weakness in the shoulder girdle, facial muscles, and trunk, along with a steppage gait. Cardiac function was normal with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 75%. Vital capacity decreased from 74% in the sitting position to 46% in the supine position, indicating diaphragm muscle impairment. Additionally, sniff nasal inspiratory pressure was significantly reduced at 17 cmH2O, and maximal inspiratory pressure was 12 cmH2O, indicating reduced diaphragm muscle strength.

A 54-year-old Caucasian male presented with a mucocutaneous blistering eruption that had developed over three years. The eruption included tense blisters that easily ruptured, forming painful erosions. Some older erosions had healed with small atrophic scars and multiple milia cysts. The patient reported increased skin fragility, with lesions easily induced by minor injuries. The lesions were widespread, particularly affecting areas prone to repetitive trauma: palmoplantar regions, elbows, knees, and posterior trunk. Physical examination revealed onychodystrophy with partial loss of the big right toenail and moderate fibrosis of the fingers, resulting in reduced hand mobility. The patient also had multiple oral erosions. Previous medical records indicated an initial diagnosis based on direct immunofluorescence studies showing deposition of immunoglobulin G (IgG) and C3 at the DEJ in a linear pattern. A comprehensive metabolic panel was within normal limits. Tests for pemphigoid circulating antibodies (BPAG 180 and BPAG230) and antinuclear antibodies (ANA) were negative, and C3 and C4 levels were normal. An esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy revealed extensive erosions on the pharyngeal and upper-esophagus mucosa, with no stricture or stenosis detected. A colonoscopy showed no signs of inflammatory bowel disease. A thorough review of systems was entirely negative.

A 29-year-old male from Indonesia, previously without symptoms, was brought to the emergency department (ED) from a cruise ship due to shortness of breath and atrial fibrillation. He experienced shortness of breath, chest pain that worsened with breathing, and difficulty breathing while lying down for a week.

A 33-year-old male patient presented in February 2015 with decreased visual acuity in the left eye. His medical history includes a traumatic brain injury from a war explosion in January 2012, resulting in severe craniocerebral trauma with a temporal bone fracture and an epidural hematoma, which was drained three days post-admission. Upon discharge two months later, the documented conditions were traumatic brain injury due to explosion, mixed hypoacusis in the left ear (both conductive and sensorineural), posttraumatic left peripheral facial palsy, and lagophthalmos. Between 2012 and 2015, he underwent various surgeries: neurosurgical drainage of the hematoma, eight ENT surgeries from 2012 to 2014 for ear drum reconstruction, myringotomy, and removal of bone fragments narrowing the ear meatus, and ophthalmological procedures including total blepharorrhaphy, partial opening of the blepharorrhaphy in March 2013, and total opening of the blepharorrhaphy in December 2014.

Patient_22, a male child, was admitted at 1 year and 8 months old due to difficulty standing. The mother had two pregnancies and two births, with the boy having a healthy 4-year-old sister. During early pregnancy, there was a need for fetus preservation due to bleeding. He was born at 32 weeks via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 3.3 kg. The child could sit and turn over at 8 months and began speaking at 1 year and 6 months but was unable to stand independently. He exhibited a preference for shaking his head while talking. No similar features were reported in other family members. Physical examination revealed skull asymmetry and a head circumference of 48 cm. There were delays in intelligence, motor, and language development, hemifacial hypertrophy on the right side, facial asymmetry, a high forehead, hypertelorism, downturned corners of the mouth, strabismus, drooling, and protruding ears.

A 36-year-old male presented to the urology department at the age of 17 for evaluation of cryptorchidism and was subsequently referred to the endocrinology department for further management. On clinical examination, the patient was in good general health, exhibited a depressed mood, and showed no signs of dysmorphism. His weight was recorded at 81 kg, height at 160 cm, and body mass index at 31.50 kg/m². The patient had well-developed facial hair and pubic hair at stage V. The genital examination revealed a 9-cm penis (-1 SD) and a small, empty, pleated scrotal bursa. Hormonal assessment indicated elevated gonadotropin levels with FSH at 54.1 mIU/mL (normal range: 1.27-19.26) and LH at 23.9 mIU/mL (normal range: 1-7), while testosterone levels were undetectable.
